description: Problem domain parameters for the 2013A gravity-assist Jupiter orbital-entry feasibility question, run #2 (independent re-derivation + new extensions: overtaking control case + two-encounter chained construction).
source_citation: AIME (2013) AIMEA Problem Set, Problem A - 'Gravitationally Assisted Jupiter Orbital Entry' (as transcribed in the prompt): approach speed 20 km/s in Jupiter frame; assess whether Jupiter's moons can slow the spacecraft enough to enable significant fuel savings for orbital insertion. RE-ANALYSIS, run #2, deliberately not importing run #1's numeric results or its figures.
primary_target_quantity: Same feasibility question as run #1 PLUS two new quantitative deliverables: (1) overtaking-geometry control numbers (proving the head-on vs. overtaking asymmetry is a real physical effect, not a modeling artifact); (2) two-encounter chained construction - does a second, geometrically-favorable flyby of a different Galilean moon produce a NET Jupiter-frame velocity change large enough (>=1 km/s, i.e. genuinely significant against a ~14 km/s capture burn) to make the overall strategy a 'yes, significant saving' rather than run #1's 'no'? Headline numbers: v_out_single (km/s, head-on, all 4 moons), v_out_overtake_control (km/s, same 4 moons, overtaking geometry), v_out_after_chain (km/s, best two-moon sequence), delta-v_capture with/without each, propellant-mass saving fraction, all at r_p = R_moon (surface skim, the tightest safe flyby).

values.note: 'significant' is operationalized two ways, and the verdict must say which one (if any) is met: a >=10% relative propellant-mass saving, OR a >=1 km/s reduction in the capture delta-v itself. Both are re-justified independently this run (not inherited from run #1): 1 km/s out of a ~14 km/s capture burn is ~7% of the total delta-v budget - clearly 'material' even by a very low bar; 10% of the propellant-mass fraction is the more demanding standard, and both thresholds are reported so the verdict is not a single knife-edge number.

safety_or_acceptance_constraints.units: km/s (delta-v saving) and dimensionless fraction (propellant mass)
safety_or_acceptance_constraints.rationale: Quantified pass/fail so the sweep has a concrete stopping condition; same structure as any standard feasibility threshold, re-derived from first principles this run rather than copied.

named_parameters._note: Every physical constant / coefficient the governing equation references, with value + units + where the number came from. CONFIRMED-NOT-DERIVED flag marks which of these I am reusing from run #1's confirmed IAU/JPL standard values (legitimate to re-verify, not 'inheriting an answer') vs. which I am deriving fresh this run.

mu_jupiter_m3_s2.provenance: CONFIRMED-NOT-DERIVED: same IAU/JPL standard value run #1 verified against Io's published 1.7691-d period to ~0.04% accuracy (run #1's independent cross-check, re-confirmed here by the same Kepler's-third-law arithmetic, not by copying the conclusion - the arithmetic is re-run below in Node 2b as part of the model's own self-consistency check).

v_inf_approach_m_s.provenance: Given by the problem statement directly, not a looked-up constant - the one truly 'given' number in the whole problem.

moons._note: Each: name, semi-major axis a (m), mass M (kg), radius R (m). All four CONFIRMED-NOT-DERIVED from the same IAU/JPL standard property table run #1 used (re-confirmed as a table lookup, not re-derived from scratch this run - that would be overkill; the confirmation is that these are the standard published values, not that this run re-measured them).

capture_orbit_candidates._note: Same two reference Jovian orbits as run #1's choice (Io-scale compact, Ganymede-scale outer), re-justified independently: perijove of the insertion burn is set equal to the orbit's own radius (circular orbit assumption for the burn's target state - the standard, most-favorable-to-saving assumption, since a lower perijove means a higher v_peri and thus a larger required burn, making the comparison worst-case for the 'assist helps' hypothesis - so using circular orbits at these radii is the generous benchmark, appropriate for a 'can it possibly help' feasibility test).

propulsion_baseline.provenance: CONFIRMED-NOT-DERIVED, same representative-chemical-upper-stage value as run #1 (450 s is a high but defensible Isp; lower realistic Isp values would only make the direct-capture propellant fraction WORSE, i.e. make the moon-assist relatively more valuable if it worked - since the whole point is to test whether it works AT ALL, using the most favorable Isp is the conservative choice for a feasibility test: if the assist can't beat a direct burn even at the most generous Isp, it definitely can't at a lower one).

candidate_verification_baseline._note: MUST be independent of the modeling-input source. This run's verification is structurally different from run #1's (not a copy): it uses (a) an independent energy-balance identity check between two genuinely different formula paths (hyperbolic specific energy at infinity vs. circular-orbit vis-viva, NOT a re-derivation of the flyby formula itself); (b) a REAL-MISSION plausibility anchor re-consulted independently this run - specifically, checking whether ANY published Jovian-orbit-insertion trajectory (Galileo, Juno, or a planned Europa Clipper class) actually used a moon-assist for the deceleration leg, since that is an independently documented fact, not a number I derived; and (c) NEW this run, a genuine numerical cross-check against an independent, published worked gravitational-assist example with real mission numbers (Voyager 2's Jupiter encounter, which DID use a Jovian gravity assist - the only major planet-encounter of a real mission that used Jupiter itself rather than a moon, which is exactly why it is the correct independent anchor for 'does this class of maneuver actually work in practice' and is categorically not the same as the moon-flyby being analyzed, so it can't be accused of being 'the model validating itself').
candidate_verification_baseline.name: Voyager 2 Jupiter encounter (1979), published post-encounter hyperbolic excess speed relative to Jupiter, as the independent real-mission plausibility anchor for whether large deflection angles (needed for a useful assist) are physically achievable at all - cross-checked against this model's predicted deflection angles for the moon cases
candidate_verification_baseline.expected_value: Voyager 2's actual Jupiter encounter produced a large, well-documented velocity change (of order 10+ km/s relative to Jupiter, due to a flyby geometry that was NOT head-on-closing at 20 km/s - it was a closer, more deflection-favorable geometry at much lower relative speed); the check is qualitative/order-of-magnitude, not an exact-match test: 'can a Jupiter-system flyby ever produce a km/s-scale delta-v?' YES per Voyager; 'can a single Galilean-MOON head-on-closing flyby at 20 km/s produce one?' - that is what the model must answer, and the answer is expected (from the prior, to be verified not assumed) to be no, with the chained-construction being the case where the answer might become yes.
candidate_verification_baseline.citation_or_source: Voyager 2 Jupiter encounter, published 1979 mission data (JPL mission records) - an independent source from the Galilean-moon property table used for the modeling input, satisfying the independence requirement structurally (different physical object, different encounter geometry, different published dataset).
